question.text: What is the concept of a 'Politically Exposed Person (PEP)' in AML/CFT compliance?

answer.text: An individual who is or has been entrusted with a prominent public function in a foreign country or domestically
Any person who donates to political parties above a specified threshold
A government employee at any level who handles public funds
A person who has been convicted of a politically motivated crime

explanation.text: The Logic: The international AML/CFT standard (FATF) defines a Politically Exposed Person as an individual who is or has been entrusted with a prominent public function, whether in a foreign country or domestically. Typical examples include heads of state, senior politicians, senior government, judicial or military officials, senior executives of state-owned enterprises, and important political party officials. PEP status triggers enhanced due diligence, senior-management approval for the relationship, and source-of-funds/source-of-wealth checks. A general government employee, a political donor, or someone convicted of a politically motivated crime is not, by that fact alone, a PEP. The Trap: Not every government employee is a PEP — only those in prominent positions. Political donors are not PEPs simply by virtue of making donations. Note: A direct "prominent public function" definition of PEPs, framed as foreign or domestic, is not stated on the NISM Series XXIV AML and CFT Provisions in Securities Markets workbook pages checked (which list PEPs as a special-category client requiring EDD and risk systems); the framing above reflects the FATF/general AML standard definition rather than a workbook citation.
